podcast.title: Kent State Shootings' Profound Impact (1970)
podcast.body: Joe Walsh, who majored in English and minored in music, stated that being at the shootings "affected me profoundly." This experience led him to view college differently and ultimately influenced his decision to pursue music as a full-time profession as the James Gang gained momentum, concluding, "I decided that maybe I don't need a degree that bad." "Unfortunately, I was at the shootings. After that, I didn't look at college the same. Then the James Gang started to gather momentum and I decided I'd try pursuing music as a profession."

podcast.title: Kent State Student on May 4, 1970
podcast.body: Joe Walsh, despite having already released two records with the James Gang and being on the verge of touring with The Who, was enrolled in classes at Kent State on May 4, 1970, and was present during the shootings. He first enrolled in 1965, attending full-time for less than a year, then part-time for about six years. "I think we were still making the blueprint for what it meant to be a rock star. It's kind of like the major league baseball players who had to take jobs to sell appliances or life insurance or something like that in the off season."

podcast.title: Presidential Candidacy (1980)
podcast.body: Joe Walsh ran for president in 1980, pledging to make his song "Life's Been Good" the new national anthem. His intention was to raise awareness about the importance of voting among the younger generation. "Jo Walsh ran for president in 1980, and he vowed to make life spend good, the new national anthem. That would have been interesting."

podcast.title: Recollection of Shootings (2020)
podcast.body: In a 2020 Facebook post, Joe Walsh graphically recalled the Kent State shootings, emphasizing that those present remembered the day vividly. He described the students as "naive young people" peacefully demonstrating, whose situation mutated into violence due to "total dysfunctional authority" that did not understand how to handle it. "those of us who were there, remember that day graphically when our classmates, our friends got shut down."

podcast.title: "The Phantom of Kent State"
podcast.body: In a 1975 interview with Guitar World magazine, Joe Walsh described himself as "the phantom of Kent State" because he pursued an unconventional assortment of classes, including music theory, electronics, and welding, during his time at the university. "In a 1975 interview with Qatar World magazine, Walsh described himself as the, quote, phantom of Kent state that meant he took kind of an odd assortment of classes like music theory, electronics, welding, things like that."

xref.title: Taylor Hawkins and the Co-Tale Riders (2006)
xref.body: In 2006, Taylor Hawkins formed his own band, Taylor Hawkins and the Co-Tale Riders, a name reflecting his sense of humor and humbleness. The band featured crack session musicians and released three albums, collaborating with figures like Roger Taylor and Brian May (Queen), Nancy Wilson (Heart), Joe Walsh (Eagles), Chrissie Hynde (Pretenders), and LeAnn Rimes. "The first came in 2006 when he formed a band called Taylor Hawkins and the Co-Tale Riders."

xref.title: Taylor Hawkins' Lead Vocals
xref.body: Taylor Hawkins was the only member other than Dave Grohl to sing lead on Foo Fighters songs. He sang on covers like Pink Floyd's "Have a Cigar" (with Brian May on guitar), Cream's "I Feel Fine," and Joe Walsh's "Life of Illusion," as well as original songs like "Cold Day in the Sun" and "Sunday Rain." "Just to show you how special a place Taylor Hawkins had within the food fighters, he is the only guy other than Dave Grohl to sing lead on a food song."
